blocks.text: Picture a spreadsheet someone hands you with a row for every product and a separate column for every single month, jan_sales, feb_sales, mar_sales, and so on marching off to the right. It looks tidy at a glance, but the moment you try to plot it or feed it into a model, it fights you. Melt is the pandas function that fixes exactly this problem, and understanding it is really just understanding one idea: turning columns into rows.
1. Introduction

pd.melt() takes a wide DataFrame, one row per entity with many columns holding different measurements or time periods, and reshapes it into a long DataFrame, one row per entity per measurement, with a new column recording which measurement it is and another column holding the actual value. Nothing about the underlying data changes. Only its shape does.

blocks.alt: A product row branching out into three separate spread out columns, jan_sales, feb_sales, mar_sales
blocks.caption: This is wide format: one row per product, one column per month.

blocks.text: If you already know pivot_table, you have a huge head start here, because melt is its exact inverse. Pivoting takes long data and spreads it wide, grouping values into new columns. Melting takes wide data and stacks it back down into rows. They are two names for opposite directions of the same trip, and thinking of melt that way will make every parameter in this lesson click faster.

blocks.alt: Wide DataFrame turning into Long DataFrame through melt, and Long DataFrame turning back into Wide DataFrame through pivot_table
blocks.caption: Melt and pivot_table are mirror images of each other, one direction each.

blocks.title: Melt in one sentence
blocks.content: Melt collapses a group of columns into two columns, one naming which original column a value came from, one holding that value, while repeating everything else you told it to keep.

blocks.text: 2. Wide Format vs Long Format

Before touching the melt function itself, it helps to be able to spot wide and long format on sight, since melt only makes sense once the difference is second nature. Take a tiny sales table with three products and three months of sales as the running example for this whole lesson.
2.1 What Wide Format Looks Like

That table above is wide format. Each product gets exactly one row, and every month of sales gets its own column sitting off to the right. As more months get added, the table keeps growing sideways rather than downward, which is the telltale sign of wide data: the number of columns depends on how many time periods or measurements you happen to have.

blocks.alt: A wide sales table branching into one row per product and a separate column per month
blocks.caption: Wide format grows sideways, one new column for every new month.

blocks.text: 2.2 What Long Format Looks Like

The long version of that exact same data drops the one-column-per-month setup entirely. Instead you get one row for every single product-and-month combination, with a column naming which month that row refers to and another column holding the sales number for it.

Same underlying numbers, completely different shape. Nine rows instead of three, but only three columns instead of four, and it keeps growing downward rather than sideways as more months arrive. That growing-downward-not-sideways habit is the signature of long format.

blocks.alt: A Long DataFrame branching into a variable column, a value column, and one row per observation
blocks.caption: Long format keeps a fixed number of columns and adds rows instead.

blocks.text: 2.3 Why Long Format Is What You Actually Need

Wide format is genuinely nice for humans to skim, which is exactly why spreadsheets default to it. But most real analysis work, plotting especially, wants long format instead, because it expects one row per observation, not one row per entity with a pile of related columns spread out next to it.

items: Plotting libraries like matplotlib and seaborn generally want a single column to map to color, a single column to map to the x-axis, and a single column to map to the y-axis, which only exists cleanly once your months live in one column instead of three.
Groupby and aggregation get simpler on long data, since grouping by the month column is one line, versus writing separate logic for jan_sales, feb_sales, and mar_sales individually.
Many ML preprocessing steps, scalers, encoders, and most model training loops, expect one row per observation, not one row per entity carrying several observations squashed into different columns.

blocks.alt: Wide DataFrame feeding awkwardly into a plotting library while a Long DataFrame feeds cleanly into the same library
blocks.caption: Long format is what most plotting calls and preprocessing steps actually expect.

blocks.title: A quick smell test
blocks.content: If you catch yourself about to write a separate line of plotting or aggregation code for jan_sales, then feb_sales, then mar_sales, that repetition is usually a sign you should have melted the data first instead.

blocks.text: 3. The Core Parameters of pd.melt
Once the wide-to-long mental picture is solid, the parameters of pd.melt() stop being abstract names and start mapping directly onto pieces of that picture.

code.content:
pd.melt(
    df,
    id_vars=None,
    value_vars=None,
    var_name=None,
    value_name='value'
)

blocks.text: 3.1 id_vars: The Columns That Stay Put

id_vars lists the columns that should not get touched. These are the identifying columns, product_name in the running example, and melt repeats each one's value for every new row it creates out of that same original row.

blocks.alt: An id_vars column repeating unchanged across three separate rows
blocks.caption: id_vars columns stay exactly as they are and just get repeated down the new rows.

blocks.text: 3.2 value_vars: The Columns That Get Unpivoted

value_vars lists the columns that should get unpivoted into rows, jan_sales, feb_sales, and mar_sales in the running example. Each one turns into its own row per original entity, with its column name and its value peeled apart into the two new columns.

blocks.alt: Three separate spread out columns, jan_sales, feb_sales, mar_sales, all funneling into new rows
blocks.caption: value_vars columns get unpivoted, each one becoming its own row.

blocks.title: Leaving value_vars out entirely
blocks.content: If you skip value_vars, pandas melts every single column that is not listed in id_vars, automatically. That is convenient when you genuinely want everything else unpivoted, but it is an easy way to accidentally melt a column you meant to keep, so it is worth being explicit whenever the DataFrame has columns you are not fully sure about.

blocks.text: 3.3 var_name and value_name: Naming the New Columns

Left on their own, the two brand new columns melt creates are called variable and value, generic names that work but rarely read well. var_name renames the column holding the original column names, and value_name renames the column holding the actual numbers.

blocks.alt: A generic variable column renamed to month and a generic value column renamed to sales
blocks.caption: var_name and value_name swap the generic defaults for names that actually describe the data.

code.content:
pd.melt(
    df,
    id_vars=['product_name'],
    value_vars=['jan_sales', 'feb_sales', 'mar_sales'],
    var_name='month',
    value_name='sales'
)

blocks.text: 4. Worked Example: Melting Wide Sales Data
Time to run the whole thing end to end on the sales table from earlier, starting with the wide DataFrame and ending with a clean long one.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'product_name': ['Keyboard', 'Monitor', 'Mouse'],
    'jan_sales': [120, 80, 200],
    'feb_sales': [135, 95, 180],
    'mar_sales': [150, 70, 210],
})
print(df)

blocks.text: That is the DataFrame from before, three rows, four columns, sales spread wide across three separate month columns. Now melt it, keeping product_name as the identifying column and renaming the two new columns to month and sales.

code.content:
df_long = pd.melt(
    df,
    id_vars=['product_name'],
    value_vars=['jan_sales', 'feb_sales', 'mar_sales'],
    var_name='month',
    value_name='sales'
)
print(df_long)

blocks.alt: jan_sales, feb_sales, and mar_sales columns funneling into a single month column and a single sales column
blocks.caption: Three wide sales columns become one month column and one sales column, nine long rows total.

blocks.text: Three products times three months gives nine rows, exactly as expected, since melt creates one new row for every original row and value_vars column pair. Notice the order too: pandas walks through value_vars column by column, so all three products appear for jan_sales first, then all three again for feb_sales, and so on.

blocks.title: Watch the row order
blocks.content: Melt does not sort the result by product_name or by month. It just walks through value_vars in the order you gave them. If you need a specific row order for a chart or a report, sort df_long explicitly afterward rather than assuming melt already did it.

blocks.text: 5. The Round Trip: Melt and pivot_table

Since melt and pivot_table are inverses, running one after the other should land you back close to where you started. Proving that to yourself is one of the fastest ways to make the relationship between the two feel concrete instead of theoretical.
5.1 Melting Then Pivoting Back

Start from the original wide sales table, melt it down to long format the way the worked example just did, and then pivot that long table back with product_name as the index and month as the new columns. Conceptually, that trip should recover something very close to the original wide shape.

blocks.alt: An original wide table turning into a long table through melt, then the long table turning back into a recovered wide table through pivot_table
blocks.caption: Melt down, then pivot_table back up, arrives close to where you started.

blocks.text: 5.2 Demonstrating It With Code
Picking up df_long from the worked example, pivot_table rebuilds a wide table from it.

code.content:
df_wide_again = df_long.pivot_table(
    index='product_name',
    columns='month',
    values='sales'
).reset_index()
print(df_wide_again)

blocks.text: Same nine numbers, same three products, same three months, back in wide form. It is close to the original, not necessarily byte identical to it: the column order came out alphabetical, feb_sales before jan_sales before mar_sales, instead of the calendar order from the original df.

blocks.title: Why it is close and not always exact
blocks.content: pivot_table sorts columns alphabetically by default and its aggfunc defaults to mean, so if the long data ever had more than one row per product-and-month combination, the round trip would silently average them together instead of complaining. For a clean one-to-one round trip, reorder the columns back to your preferred order afterward and make sure there really is only one value per group before pivoting.

blocks.text: 6. pd.wide_to_long: A Specialized Cousin

Melt handles any set of columns you hand it, whatever their names happen to be. Pandas also ships pd.wide_to_long(), a narrower cousin built for one specific and extremely common naming pattern: a group of columns that share a common prefix followed by a varying suffix, like sales_jan, sales_feb, sales_mar rather than jan_sales, feb_sales, mar_sales.

blocks.alt: Columns sharing a common prefix feeding into pd.wide_to_long and producing a Long DataFrame
blocks.caption: wide_to_long is built for one specific naming pattern: shared prefix, varying suffix.

code.content:
pd.wide_to_long(
    df,
    stubnames='sales',
    i='product_name',
    j='month',
    sep='_'
)

blocks.text: It infers the suffix automatically from the column names instead of you spelling out value_vars by hand, which is a nice shortcut exactly when your columns already follow that prefix-suffix convention. It is not covered in depth in this lesson, just worth knowing it exists so you reach for it instead of hand rolling something more complicated when your columns happen to fit that shape.
7. Summary

items: Melt turns wide data, one row per entity with many spread out columns, into long data, one row per entity per measurement.
id_vars are the columns that stay put and get repeated down the new rows.
value_vars are the columns that get unpivoted into rows, and if you leave value_vars out, every column not in id_vars gets melted automatically.
var_name and value_name rename the two generic new columns, variable and value, into something that actually describes your data.
Melt and pivot_table are exact inverses of each other, and melting then pivoting back should recover something close to the original wide shape.
pd.wide_to_long is a narrower cousin for columns that share a common prefix and a varying suffix.

blocks.text: Reach for melt any time a DataFrame is spread out sideways and you need it stacked into rows instead, whether that is to feed a plotting library, run a groupby, or hand clean observation rows to a model.
